name: AP Chemistry
overview: AP Chemistry is a first-year college general chemistry course. The exam tests whether you can connect particle-level models (atoms, bonds, intermolecular forces, collisions) to measurable properties and data, and carry out multi-step quantitative reasoning: stoichiometry, gas laws, kinetics, equilibrium, pH, thermochemistry, and electrochemistry. Questions are built on particulate diagrams, data tables, graphs, and lab scenarios; pure recall is rare.
examMode: Hybrid digital: multiple-choice is taken in the Bluebook app; free-response questions are viewed in Bluebook and answers are handwritten in a paper booklet.

sections.name: Section I
sections.notes: Mix of discrete questions and sets built on a shared stimulus (data, particulate diagrams, lab descriptions). A periodic table and equation sheet are provided.

sections.name: Section II
sections.questionType: Free response: 3 long (10 pts each) + 4 short (4 pts each)
sections.notes: Long questions are multi-part and usually span several units, often built around a lab or data set. Suggested pacing ~23 min per long question and ~9 min per short question.

skills.name: 1. Models and Representations
skills.description: Describe and explain chemical phenomena using particulate models, Lewis diagrams, and other representations.

skills.name: 2. Question and Method
skills.description: Identify testable questions, hypotheses, procedures, and sources of error in experiments.

skills.name: 3. Representing Data and Phenomena
skills.description: Represent chemical phenomena with equations, graphs, and diagrams.

skills.name: 4. Model Analysis
skills.description: Analyze and interpret models and explain their limitations.

skills.name: 5. Mathematical Routines
skills.description: Solve problems with mathematical relationships: stoichiometry, gas laws, rate laws, equilibrium, pH, ΔG, cell potential.

skills.name: 6. Argumentation
skills.description: Develop explanations or scientific arguments using claims, evidence, and particle-level reasoning.

scoring.summary: Section I (60 MCQ, 1 raw point each, no guessing penalty) and Section II (46 raw points: 3 × 10 + 4 × 4) are each scaled to 50% of a weighted composite, which College Board converts to a 1–5 score using cut points set each year. Partial credit on FRQs is generous: a correct method with a carried-forward error still earns most points.

frqTypes.name: Long FRQ
frqTypes.howScored: Multi-part question (often a lab or data set) spanning several units. Points awarded per element: correct calculation with setup and units, correct claim plus particle-level justification, correct representation (Lewis diagram, particulate drawing, graph). Errors carried forward are not penalized twice.

frqTypes.name: Short FRQ
frqTypes.howScored: Usually 3–4 parts on one topic. One point per correct calculation, justified claim, or representation.

strategy: Budget about 90 seconds per MCQ; skip and flag any long calculation and return to it.
Estimate before computing: most MCQ answer choices differ by a factor of 2, 10, or a sign, so a rough calculation often decides it.
On FRQs, always show the setup with units; a correct setup with an arithmetic slip still earns points.
Justifications must reference particles: 'stronger London dispersion forces because larger, more polarizable electron cloud', not 'bigger molecule'.
For any 'explain' about a property, name the specific interaction (ion–dipole, hydrogen bonding, Coulombic attraction) and compare it between the two substances.
Use Q vs. K to predict shifts; it is more reliable than memorized Le Châtelier rules.
Write net ionic equations: drop spectator ions and keep weak acids, weak bases, solids, gases, and water as molecules.
Answer each part independently; a later part often doesn't need an earlier answer, or lets you use a carried-forward value.
pitfalls: Saying bonds break during boiling; phase changes overcome intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.
Thinking bond breaking releases energy; breaking bonds always absorbs energy.
Treating a catalyst as shifting equilibrium or changing ΔH; it only lowers activation energy for both directions.
Confusing strong vs. concentrated, and weak vs. dilute, for acids.
Using the wrong sign convention for q, ΔH, and work, or forgetting to convert J to kJ.
Including solids or pure liquids in equilibrium expressions.
Assuming every reaction with negative ΔH is thermodynamically favored; check ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
Explaining periodic trends with 'wants to fill its octet' instead of Coulomb's law (effective nuclear charge and distance).
referenceSheet: A periodic table and an equations and constants sheet are provided in both sections. It includes: atomic structure (E = hν, c = λν); equilibrium (Kc, Kp, Ka, Kb, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, pH = −log[H⁺], pH + pOH = 14, pKa = −log Ka, Henderson–Hasselbalch); kinetics (integrated rate laws for zero, first, and second order, t½ = 0.693/k for first order); gases, liquids, and solutions (PV = nRT, Dalton's law, KE = ½mv², M = n/V, A = εbc); thermodynamics and electrochemistry (q = mcΔT, ΔS°, ΔH°, ΔG° as sums over products minus reactants, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, ΔG° = −RT ln K, ΔG° = −nFE°, I = q/t); constants (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K), F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻, Avogadro's number, Planck's constant, speed of light).
